description: MarsLayer is focused on Jezero Crater and the Martian Map challenge. It explores how orbital imagery, topographic data, geological context, and mission evidence can be brought together in an accessible field-guide interface. The current experience demonstrates CTX imagery, DTM terrain visualization, geographic selection, and native-pixel elevation inspection. MarsLayer is an exploratory science interface designed to help users investigate Martian terrain and its geological context.
summary:
MarsLayer is an evidence-aware planetary exploration environment focused on Jezero Crater, Mars. It connects exploration of a planetary landscape with the scientific record behind it through CTX imagery, native digital terrain model elevation sampling, field-stop exploration, coordinate entry, provenance, and explicit scientific limitations. 

Rather than treating visualization as measurement, MarsLayer distinguishes observation, derived analysis, and scientific interpretation. A verified reference measurement at 18.509°N, 77.256°E returns −2244.53125 m using the nearest containing native DTM pixel without interpolation. 

The project demonstrates how planetary exploration interfaces can make NASA data more accessible while preserving evidence boundaries, reproducibility, and uncertainty.
details:
MarsLayer provides an interactive scientific exploration workflow for Jezero Crater. Users can examine CTX imagery and elevation views, explore three field stops, enter coordinates, and obtain elevation measurements through native CTX DTM sampling. The interface exposes source, method, provenance, and limitation information so that visualization, numerical measurement, and scientific interpretation remain distinct.

The project uses CTX imagery at 6 m/pixel and a separate CTX DTM product at 20 m/pixel. The verified Neretva reference sample at 18.509°N, 77.256°E returns −2244.53125 m at pixel column 283, row 628, using the nearest containing native DTM pixel without interpolation.

MarsLayer intentionally communicates evidence boundaries. A point measurement does not establish regional accuracy; elevation visualization is not itself numerical measurement or a route-safety assessment; exact CTX imagery/DTM pixel registration has not been established; and DTM vertical-reference compatibility with MOLA has not been established.

MOLA integration remains deferred and is not presented as an implemented application capability.

The intended impact is to make planetary exploration more accessible without sacrificing scientific transparency:

EXPLORE → OBSERVE → INVESTIGATE → UNDERSTAND.
